title: Tests: database, worker and fault checks
summary: This area holds the repository's strongest behavioral evidence in its least maintained code. tests/db has 75 files and 10,793 lines: 43 scripts that print JSON cases for scripts/app_db.py and the scripts/qualify_*.py qualifiers, plus the workers they kill, browser-suite arrangements, scripted models and the SQL fixtures for two disposable stacks. tests/web, tests/qualification and tests/faults add fixture servers, workers and deliberate-fault samples. What the checks exercise is excellent: real Postgres through the runtime role, real Storage with member tokens, real SIGKILL and SIGSTOP at chosen points, scripted models over fake transports, and leak scans of stored state and logs. How they are built is weak. No shared check module exists, so the case protocol and setup are copied: 42 check() copies in 6 variants, 24 value() helpers and 39 inline statements that release every job in the database. Mains run 150 to 316 lines, one exception skips every later scenario, and 26 of the 43 scripts then print nothing. 14 files depend on 21 private product names in a folder that no linter, formatter or type checker reads. 80 checks compute the shown value and the verdict with separate calls, and with one arrangement that never isolates its guard, three claim cases can pass with the guard they test broken. Comments, docstrings and case names are a model for the rest of the repository. A small shared check module, a lint and type gate for tests/, and public names for the private helpers would make this evidence cheap to keep.

scores.why: No lint, format or type gate covers these files: 72 files would be reformatted, with 2,759 long lines and 307 suppressions for tools that never run here.
No shared check module; 14 files bind to 21 private product names, and an install helper for the real key lives in tests/db.
35 functions run over 80 lines, 19 over 150 and 10 over 200; most are mains made of long scenario lists.
Each main arranges, acts, asserts and emits browser state in one body, and each file recreates its closures over db; the small helpers are clear.
75 files share one flat folder across six roles, and the _check, _live, _worker and _script suffixes don't reliably name the role.
Real stores, processes, scripted models and fake transports are right; isolating checks by ending every job, and a hand-rolled JSON protocol in every file, are not.
Every file states its story, decision and scope, and 'Arranged' marks constructed preconditions; review IDs lack their source path.
No type checker runs; value() returns Any, and SimpleNamespace stand-ins and 10 type: ignore comments appear, three hiding values the product types forbid.
26 of 43 scripts drop observed cases on a crash, one exception skips every later scenario, and some refusal checks accept any exception.
The riskiest behavior (fencing, crashes, reconciliation, leakage) is exercised for real, but 80 checks evaluate twice and three claim cases can pass when broken.
Valuable, well-explained evidence sits in copy-pasted, unlinted 200 to 300 line scripts tied to private internals.

findings.title: Checks compute the shown value and the verdict with separate calls, so some can pass broken

locations.note: a paused run is not claimable: its run keeps a live owner, so this passes even with the pause guard removed
claim_next twice after the owner's lease expires: a wrongful first claim makes the second return None, so the case passes
the same, for a job whose available_at is in the future
shows one claim_next result and judges another
expire_due twice: the first call does the work the second is judged on
read-only example: the same generation query in both arguments
expected text says '1 check', but the predicate never checks it
a user pause leaves a live owner's lease in place, which shields line 144

findings.evidence:
check(name, expected, observed, passed) takes the shown value and the verdict as independent expressions. An ast count finds 80 calls in 20 files whose two arguments await the same call, and 5 of those calls change state: claim_next at worker_ownership_check.py:74, 144, 146 and 164, and expire_due at approval_check.py:185.
check('a paused run is not claimable', 'no claim', await claim_next(db, worker_id='x') is None, await claim_next(db, worker_id='x') is None)
At 146 and 164 only the guard under test stands between the run and a claim. If it broke, the first call would claim the run, the second would find it held and return None, and the case would show False and pass. At 144 the paused run still has a live owner, because a user pause keeps a live owner's lease (runs.py:468-476), so the case passes even with the pause guard removed. An earlier review already found 'tests that couldn't fail' (docs/engineering/evidence/REVIEW-US-5.1-to-US-9.3/fixes-majors.md:58).
findings.impact: These cases are the lease and claim evidence that python-worker.md asks for, and claim_next's eligibility lives in SQL (worker_leases.py:79-81), so these disposable cases are what proves it. Three of them (lines 144, 146 and 164) can pass with the guard they name broken, and approval_check.py:185 cannot fail at all. The other 75 double reads cost an extra query each, and can show a value other than the one judged.
findings.recommendation: Evaluate once and judge that value. Change check to take the value and a predicate, or assign the value to a variable first. Fix the five state-changing cases now, and give line 144 an arrangement in which only the pause guard stands between the run and a claim (line 146 already is one). Convert the rest when the shared module (TDBC-03) lands. Make each predicate assert what the expected text claims, which verification_check.py:97 does not for its '1 check'.
findings.sketch:
def check(self, name: str, expected: str, actual: T, ok: Callable[[T], bool] | bool) -> T:
    passed = ok(actual) if callable(ok) else ok
    self.records.append(Case(id=name, expected=expected, observed=short(actual), passed=bool(passed)))
    return actual

taken = await claim_next(db, worker_id='x')   # one call, shown and judged
cases.check('a paused run is not claimable', 'no claim', taken, lambda lease: lease is None)
findings.ruleCheck: python-worker.md asks for tests of stale ownership and duplicate delivery. The change lets those cases fail when the guard breaks; no guard, lease or check is weakened.
findings.verifierNote: Recounted with ast: 80 calls in 20 files, 5 of them state-changing. Corrected why line 144 passes: a user pause keeps the live owner's lease (runs.py:468-476), so the double call is not the cause there.

findings.title: A crash ends every later scenario, and 26 of 43 scripts then print nothing

locations.note: bare asyncio.run: a crash discards every case observed so far
same, for the review round 1 majors

findings.evidence: The 43 case-printing scripts end in three ways. 26 print nothing if they crash: 23 call asyncio.run or main() bare, and 3 are CLIs that print only on success. 15 print partial cases and re-raise, and 2 print in finally. No script isolates a scenario, so one exception skips the rest. All 26 value() copies return (await (await db.execute(sql, values)).fetchone())[0]. assignment_check.py:219-221 starts a worker that must die, never checks its exit code, and then reads child_run_id from a row that may not exist. keys_and_vars_check.py and tool_keys_check.py also refuse to print when a fixture secret reached their output (tool_keys_check.py:336-338).
findings.impact: When blocker_check.py or major_check.py crashes, the db evidence holds one 'the X check ran: exit 1' line instead of dozens of observed results. The run fails, so nothing is counted as green, but the cases observed before the crash are lost and the later scenarios are neither run nor named, which are the gaps DH-W04 asks evidence to report. For the checks app_db.py runs, partial output is discarded anyway (app_db.py:367-369).
findings.recommendation: Use one wrapper that always prints the collected cases, after the same leak scan that keys_and_vars_check.py and tool_keys_check.py run today, so a crash can never print a fixture secret. Run each independent scenario under a guard that records its exception as a failed case and moves on. Make value() raise a NoRow error that names its SQL, and record each killed worker's exit code as a case. Ask the scripts owners to parse partial output in app_db.py, as qualify_identity.py:183 already does.
findings.ruleCheck: DH-09: skipped checks never count as green, and DH-W04 records failures, errors and gaps. AGENTS.md keeps secrets out of evidence, so the wrapper keeps today's leak refusal before printing.
findings.verifierNote: Endings recounted (23 bare, 3 success-only CLIs, 15 print and re-raise, 2 finally). Added the leak refusal the wrapper must keep and app_db.py's early return at 367-369, and moved the connector citation to its finally (242).

findings.title: Checks end every job in the database so claim_next picks their own run

locations.note: 'Only this run's job is eligible': the release before each admission
the same statement, 3 times in this file
5 times in one main
uses whatever claim_next returned, without checking which run it is
orders checks around it: 'Last, so no later check's cleanup ends the runs they leave claimed'
holds a run for the browser with an 1800-second lease that the release would end
claims only its own run with claim_run: the pattern to spread

findings.evidence:
This statement runs 39 times in 27 files, counted by regex over joined string literals, and a shorter variant without the lease columns runs 3 more times in improvement_check.py:
update app_private.run_jobs set status = 'done', lease_owner = null, lease_expires_at = null where status <> 'done'
It runs mid-scenario, and it also ends live leases that other checks hold for browser suites. Only 6 of the 29 files that call claim_next assert that the claimed run is the one they admitted.
findings.impact: Adding or reordering a check can end another check's browser arrangement, as the ordering comment in qualify_identity.py shows. If an eligible job from another check survives, a scenario silently drives the wrong run. Isolation lives in 39 SQL strings instead of one named place.
findings.recommendation: Name the isolation step once. It should end only what claim_next could take, meaning queued jobs and expired leases, so live leases stay, and then assert the claimed run. Where the worker's own claim isn't under test, claim the run with claim_run and drive it with run_goal, as task_timing_check.py does.
findings.sketch:
Db.quiesce(): end only jobs claim_next could take; live leases, including browser arrangements, stay
  update app_private.run_jobs set status = 'done', lease_owner = null, lease_expires_at = null
  where status = 'queued' or (status = 'claimed' and lease_expires_at < clock_timestamp())
Db.claim(run): claim_run(run) when the worker's claim isn't the subject; otherwise quiesce(), process_next(),
  then a case asserting the run under test is the one that moved
findings.ruleCheck: DH-07 requires explicit fixture ownership, and DH-08 says cleanup proves ownership first. The narrower release touches only jobs that no live owner holds, on disposable targets only.
findings.verifierNote: Recounted 39 exact copies in 27 files plus 3 shorter ones, and 6 of 29 claim_next callers that assert the claimed run. The ordering comment is at qualify_identity.py:170, not 169.

findings.evidence: Measured from py_functions.json: 35 functions in the area exceed 80 lines (30 of them named main), 19 exceed 150 and 10 exceed 200. verification_check.main runs 316 lines through about 14 sections separated only by comments. It defines value, admit, candidate, scope_of and state as closures over db, and rebinds run, lease, model and result in each section. browser_executor_check.py already splits its work into containment, isolation and ownership functions.
findings.impact: A scenario can't be named, run or failed alone. Readers must track variable rebinding across hundreds of lines, and the first exception decides how much of the file ever runs.
findings.recommendation: Split each main into module-level scenario functions that take the shared Db and Cases, list them in a SCENARIOS tuple, and pass state between dependent scenarios explicitly. Start with the eight largest, each when it is next touched.
findings.sketch:
SCENARIOS = (publish_is_required, superseded_copy_fails, unknown_effect_blocks, stale_verifier_writes_nothing,
             backoff_retry_is_fenced, pause_lets_call_finish, interrupted_internal_writes, hung_call_is_bounded,
             exception_type_is_logged, inputs_are_read_only)   # 15 to 40 lines each

async def main(cases: Cases) -> None:
    async with Db.connect(WORKSPACE) as db:
        for scenario in SCENARIOS:
            await cases.scenario(scenario.__name__, scenario(db, cases))   # a crash is one failed case
findings.ruleCheck: DH-06 asks for small cohesive modules. No rule fixes the layout of these scripts, and the JSON cases keep their shape.
findings.verifierNote: py_functions.json gives 35 functions over 80 lines (30 named main), 19 over 150 and 10 over 200, and verification_check.main defines the five closures and about 14 comment-separated sections described.

findings.evidence: 44 files end in _check.py: 43 print cases, product_inference_check.py prints none, and operations_check.py is part CLI. Browser arrangements and live actions are spread across _live.py and unsuffixed names. *_worker.py covers both killed children and long-running serve loops, and worker_process.py is a killed worker. The synthetic H1 stack (migrations/, seeds/, bad_migrations/, worker_fixture.sql, storage_policies.sql, schema app) sits beside the application stack's app_fixture.sql and app_bad_migrations/. Paths are referenced from app_db.py, the qualify_*.py scripts and, in comments, 6 Playwright specs.
findings.impact: Readers can't tell what runs where (app_db, a qualifier or a Playwright spec), or what a new file should be called. The flat folder works only because each file runs as a script with its own folder first on sys.path, so a move into subfolders also has to give the invokers tests/db on PYTHONPATH.
findings.recommendation: Group files by role: checks/, workers/, arrange/ (browser-suite setup and live actions), fixtures/ (scripted models, sinks, graphs and the shared module), sql/h1/ and sql/app/. Add a README table mapping each file to its invoker. Give product_inference_check.py an arrangement name, and split operations_check.py's CLI from its check. Move everything in one change, together with the invoker paths and tests/db on the invokers' PYTHONPATH.
findings.ruleCheck: DH-03 lists tests/harness/ but not a layout for tests/db, so subfolders don't conflict. The SQL fixtures stay synthetic and disposable.
findings.verifierNote: Roles and counts confirmed (44 _check.py files; the 6 specs name these paths in comments). Dropped the claim that the flat layout forces the 32 sys.path inserts: they are redundant for scripts run directly.
